newsitem.title: USA: U.S. abandons legal battle on striker replacements.
newsitem.headline: U.S. abandons legal battle on striker replacements.

text.p: The Clinton administration said Monday it had abandoned a legal battle to prevent companies that permanently replace striking workers from doing business with the federal government.

Justice Department spokesman Bert Brandenburg said the government had no plans to petition the Supreme Court to overturn a lower court ruling that struck down President Clinton's executive order of March 8, 1995, against federal contractors that hire permanent replacements. Monday was the filing deadline.
"My understanding is that we have not filed anything today, and I've been told that we don't plan to file anything," Brandenberg said.

Under the order, companies that do more than $100,000 a year in business with the federal government could have had their contracts cancelled and been disqualified from future business if they hired permanent replacements for lawfully striking workers.
An administration official said the decision not to pursue the case was an effort to avoid the risk of a sweeping high court ruling that could have limited presidential power.

"There was some concern that a negative ruling from the Supreme Court could have very far-reaching implications on any president's authority to issue executive orders," the official, who asked not to be identified, said.

Labour Secretary Robert Reich, who had vigorously defended the president's order, said the administration had withdrawn from its legal battle to avoid protracted litigation but had not abandoned its efforts to improve striker protection.

"The administration will continue to explore ways to protect the rights of American workers, to promote stable collective bargaining and to ensure the efficiency of the completion of government contracts," Reich said.
Administration-backed legislation to outlaw the permanent replacement of strikers failed to pass Congress in 1994.

Before the order took effect, business groups, led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, persuaded a U.S. District Court judge to block the administration temporarily from enforcing the order while they appealed.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals unanimously overturned the president's order on Feb. 2, ruling that it conflicted with employers' rights under federal labour law to hire permanent replacements. The entire U.S. Appeals Court for the District of Columbia let the panel's ruling stand in May on a 9-2 vote.
The chamber hailed the government's decision.

"It leaves us with a tremendous victory, and it validates what we've been saying all along that the president shouldn't usurp the way laws are made, which is through the legislative process," Mona Zeiberg, the chamber's senior counsel on labour and employment law, said.
AFL-CIO General Counsel Jon Hiatt said the 76-union federation had expected the decision.

"I think it's fair to say that we don't fault the administration for this choice," he said. "When the full D.C. Circuit (Court of Appeals) denied the government's appeal, it was pretty clear to us that that was the last hope of getting anywhere through the course of this executive order."

Even though no contracts were cancelled as a result of the presidential order, the business groups said the threat of losing government business had reduced the leverage of major government contractors in contract negotiations with their workers and unions.
